claims.claim: Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ (Planetary Fact Sheet, metric): Jupiter diameter 142,984 km and mass 1898e24 kg, both the largest of the eight planets
claims.note: True as stated. The hook (A4) leaves a viewer who swipes at second two with nothing false.

claims.claim: Two and a half times the mass of every other planet combined.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ masses (1e24 kg): Mercury 0.330, Venus 4.87, Earth 5.97, Mars 0.642, Jupiter 1898, Saturn 568, Uranus 86.8, Neptune 102
claims.note: Other seven sum to 768.6e24 kg; 1898/768.6 = 2.47, which rounds to two and a half.

claims.claim: JUPITER / 2.5× the other planets / combined, by mass
claims.note: Ratio 2.47 → 2.5×, with the mass qualifier shown.

claims.claim: Row of the other seven planets beneath Jupiter at one scale: Saturn 0.833, Uranus 0.363, Neptune 0.352, Earth 0.091, Venus 0.087, Mars 0.0485, Mercury 0.035 of Jupiter's radius
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/<planet>fact.html, volumetric mean radius: Jupiter 69,911; Saturn 58,232; Uranus 25,362; Neptune 24,622; Earth 6,371.0; Venus 6,051.8; Mars 3,389.5; Mercury 2,439.7 km
claims.note: Computed 0.8330, 0.3628, 0.3522, 0.0911, 0.0866, 0.0485, 0.0349. All drawn ratios match to the shown precision.

claims.claim: But hold Jupiter up next to the Sun, and it looks tiny. (Jupiter drawn at radius 52 beside the Sun at 520)
claims.where: spoken + on-screen: Jupiter beside the Sun
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html (volumetric mean radius 695,700 km) and jupiterfact.html (69,911 km)

claims.claim: It would take nearly a thousand Jupiters to fill the Sun.
claims.note: Volume ratio 986.5, so 'nearly a thousand' is accurate. It is a volume comparison (solid spheres could not pack in that many); the on-screen 'by volume' (n7) carries that qualifier. Mass ratio check from the same sheets: 1,988,400/1,898.13 = 1,047.6, as SOURCES says.

claims.claim: ≈ 1,000 JUPITERS / to fill it, by volume / dots not to scale (1,000 small dots across the Sun's disc)
claims.source_checked: NASA Sun and Jupiter fact sheets (as n6)
claims.note: 986.5 ≈ 1,000. The visual is marked as not to scale and as a volume count, as A6 requires.

claims.claim: Our Sun is not an average star. It is an unusually big one.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985, arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source (aa-corr.tex), Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' (footnote: Sun excluded); plus the size sources listed under n9
claims.note: The Sun is larger than at least 306 of 337 typed stars within 10 pc (90.8%; see n9), so it sits in the top ~9% by size. 'Unusually big' is supported for the solar neighbourhood, and the next sentence gives that scope. The SOURCES defect in entry 4 is listed under n9.

claims.claim: It is bigger and brighter than over ninety percent of the stars in our part of the galaxy
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 (arXiv:2104.14972 source) Table 3: A 4, F 8, G 18, K 38, M 249, L 21, T 45, Y 19, D 20, N/A 41, Sun excluded; text: 41 untyped = 36 possible M, 4 possible L, 1 possible WD. Boyajian et al. 2012, ApJ 757, 112, arXiv:1208.2431 LaTeX source, table 'Fundamental Parameters' (fund_params_combined.tex). Giammichele et al. 2012, ApJS 199, 29, arXiv:1202.5581 source, Table 2 (tab2.tex, 165 WDs). Thévenin et al. 2005, A&A 436, 253, doi:10.1051/0004-6361:20042075 (Crossref record checked), arXiv:astro-ph/0501420 source: delta Eri D/D_sun = 2.33 ± 0.03. CDS J/A+A/650/A201 refused by the proxy.
claims.note: The spoken claim holds: K (except delta Eri), M and WD = 306 of 337 typed stars = 90.8% worst case; adding the 41 untyped companions gives 347/378 = 91.8%. Boyajian K dwarfs ≤ 0.831 R_sun and ≤ 0.53 L_sun; M dwarfs ≤ 0.577 R_sun and ≤ 0.070 L_sun; Giammichele brightest WD log L = -1.12, Sirius B -1.53, largest R from Teff and L 0.0216 R_sun. The spoken line needs no change. Fix the SOURCES block, entry 4 (A1/A3: it must quote the source correctly): (a) the Boyajian radii and luminosities are in the 'Fundamental Parameters' table, which is Table 6 of the paper (in both source order and callout order); Table 3 is 'Angular Diameters of K and M Dwarfs' and has no radii or luminosities. (b) 'the largest the K0 V stars GJ 702A (0.831), GJ 75 (0.819) and GJ 631 (0.759)' is wrong for GJ 631: GJ 166A (K1 V, 0.806), GJ 105 (K3 V, 0.795), GJ 764 (K0 V, 0.778) and GJ 892 (K3 V, 0.778) are all larger than GJ 631; list the two largest only, or the correct third. Not verified (catalogue blocked): that delta Eri is the only evolved K star in Reylé's 38, and the '95% counting only G0-G2 and evolved G stars' figure. Neither matters, because the worst case already counts delta Eri and needs 3 or more further exceptions to fall below 90%.

claims.claim: THE SUN / bigger than 9 stars in 10 / dots: star type, not size
claims.where: on-screen: THE SUN tag over the 100-dot grid
claims.note: The figure is right (90.8 to 91.8%), but the label drops the scope. The source is a census of stars within 10 pc; the spoken line says 'in our part of the galaxy', but a frame or screenshot of this label says it of all stars. A3 calls for the narrower claim. Change the sub to e.g. 'bigger than 9 in 10 nearby stars' (or 'stars near us'). 'dots: star type, not size' is correct.

claims.claim: because most stars are red dwarfs: small, dim, and everywhere.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 (arXiv:2104.14972 source): Table 3 M = 249; text '249 M stars among the 423 objects with a measured spectral type ... 58.9 ± 5.8%', and 61.3 ± 5.9% with the estimated types. Boyajian et al. 2012 (arXiv:1208.2431) Fundamental Parameters table.
claims.note: Spoken wording is supported: M = 249 of 337 typed stars (73.9%), and 58.9% even counting brown dwarfs. Scoped by context, following 'in our part of the galaxy'. Fix the SOURCES block, entry 5: 'M dwarfs 0.19-0.58 R_sun and 0.003-0.07 L_sun' misquotes the table, which includes GJ 551 (Proxima, M5.5 V) at 0.141 R_sun and 0.00155 L_sun. Correct it to 0.14-0.58 R_sun and 0.0016-0.07 L_sun, and the table to Table 6 (see n9).

claims.claim: 10×10 grid: 8 large bright yellow (G or hotter), 10 orange (K), 5 tiny white (white dwarfs), 77 red (M or untyped)
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 Table 3 and section on the 41 untyped objects (arXiv:2104.14972 source)
claims.note: Per 379 (337 typed + 41 untyped + Sun): G-or-hotter 31 → 8.2, K 38 → 10.0, D 20 → 5.3, M + untyped 290 → 76.5, so 8/10/5/77 sums to 100. Caveats within rounding: the 41 untyped include 4 possible L and 1 possible WD (M only = 285 → 75.2 dots), and the 21 typed L objects are left out. Neither changes the picture. 'Yellow' for A/F stars is a class-group colour; the screen says 'star type'.

claims.claim: So look at the nearest star to our own. Proxima Centauri ... The closest star to the Sun
claims.source_checked: Anglada-Escudé et al. 2016, Nature 536, 437, doi:10.1038/nature19106, arXiv:1609.03449 LaTeX source (main_final.tex l.127-129): 'At a distance of 1.295 parsecs, the red-dwarf Proxima Centauri ... is the Sun's closest stellar neighbour'

claims.claim: just over four light years away
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars where hostname like 'Proxima%': sy_dist 1.30119 (+0.00034/-0.00035) pc; Anglada-Escudé 2016: 1.295 pc
claims.note: 1.30119 pc = 4.244 ly; 1.295 pc = 4.22 ly. Both are 'just over four'.

claims.claim: and you have almost certainly never seen it. It is almost always too faint for your eyes.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars: sy_vmag 11.01. Howard et al. 2018, ApJL 860, L30, doi:10.3847/2041-8213/aacaf3, arXiv:1804.02001 LaTeX source (proxima.tex l.46, l.83)
claims.note: Howard: 'no M-dwarfs are usually visible to the naked-eye'; Proxima is 'an 11.4 g′ magnitude star' that during the 2016 superflare 'briefly became a g′=6.8 star, at the limit of visibility to trained observers at very dark sites'. That supports 'too faint' and the 'almost' hedges.

claims.claim: PROXIMA CENTAURI / ≈ 1/7 the Sun's radius (red dot flies out of the grid; drawn at 13.7 against the Sun's 96)
claims.source_checked: Kervella et al. 2017, A&A 598, L7, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201629930, arXiv:1611.03495 source: interferometric R = 0.141 ± 0.007 R_sun (Demory et al. 2009); adopted model value 0.1542 ± 0.0045. Anglada-Escudé 2016: 'a measured radius of 0.14 R_sun'. Boyajian 2012 Fundamental Parameters: GJ 551 0.1410 ± 0.0070. Exoplanet Archive st_rad 0.141 ± 0.021 (Suárez Mascareño et al. 2025). Archive st_spectype M5.5 V.
claims.note: 1/7 = 0.143, inside the measured range; 13.7/96 = 0.143. SOURCES records the 0.154 model value as A3 asks. Proxima is M5.5 V, so a red dot is right.

claims.claim: That is what most of the stars around us look like. (the 8 bright dots fade out)
claims.source_checked: Exoplanet Archive (Proxima M5.5 V); Reylé et al. 2021 Table 3 (M 249 of 337 typed, 73.9%); Howard et al. 2018 l.46 ('no M-dwarfs are usually visible to the naked-eye')
claims.note: Most nearby stars are M dwarfs like Proxima, and none of them is normally visible to the eye. 'Around us' carries the 10 pc scope.

claims.claim: The star we call ordinary is one of the rare big ones. (Sun shrinks into the grid as one of the 8; 'THE SUN / one of the few')
claims.where: spoken + on-screen: THE SUN / one of the few
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021 Table 3: A 4 + F 8 + G 18 + Sun = 31 of 379 (8.2%)
claims.note: The Sun is in the ~8% G-or-hotter group and is larger than over 90% of nearby stars (n9), so 'one of the rare big ones' and 'one of the few' hold.
